analysis.title: AI wobble about deployment, not demand (Equities Monthly, Nov 2026)
key_insights: October shifted the equity debate from whether AI demand is strong to how fast the infrastructure (power, permitting, construction) can be built. Fidelity's semiconductor analysts still see strong demand with capacity constrained in advanced processors, memory and other components.

Risk is that chip production temporarily runs ahead of data centres securing power and coming online. This could flatten and extend the AI cycle and pressure near-term semiconductor estimates and highly leveraged infrastructure providers.

Higher cost of capital raised the hurdle for equity returns. Rising capital intensity, weaker free cash flow and greater reliance on debt increased scrutiny of AI investment, and political and local resistance to data-centre development adds a constraint.

US: S&P 500 fell for a second consecutive month and the Nasdaq had its weakest month since March 2025. The equal-weighted S&P 500 outperformed the cap-weighted index and small caps edged higher. Semiconductor and memory stocks fell sharply, Alphabet and Meta lagged.
Fidelity reads the US correction as scrutiny of valuations, capital intensity and monetisation, not weaker structural demand, citing strong cloud growth and expanding hyperscaler backlogs.

S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth is around 30% with most companies beating. Revisions remain positive in the US, Japan and Taiwan, but smaller surprises mean a beat alone may not be enough where valuations discount exceptional growth.
Leadership broadened in October: equal-weight, value and defensive exposures beat growth. Momentum fell 10.2% (local) and Growth 4.9% over the month while Value rose 1.7%.

Europe: STOXX 600 gained 1.9% and outperformed the US on defensive and value rotation. Earnings growth was around 28%, concentrated in energy and technology, with only 42% of companies beating. Weak Chinese demand weighed on autos and luxury.

Europe: the ECB's October hold leaves further tightening possible if price pressures persist. German manufacturing is starting to benefit from infrastructure and defence spending, while France faces fiscal and political uncertainty with sovereign spreads wider vs Germany.

Asia Pacific fell 6.1% and APxJ fell 8.2% (trading desk section; the market review cites 6.9% for APxJ). South Korea and Taiwan were among the weakest. Fidelity sees de-rating more than deterioration, as forward earnings expectations kept rising in Korea, Taiwan and Japan.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix commentary pointed to robust high-bandwidth memory demand and tight capacity.
Taiwan shows strong revision momentum. Korea's correction looks more severe than its fundamentals imply.

Japan: BoJ held at 1.25% after September's hike with a bias toward further normalisation. A more hawkish BoJ adds currency and rates risk, while revisions and governance reform stay supportive. Main risk is a disorderly reflation path from yen weakness, higher oil or Middle East disruption.
China and Hong Kong: property support is directionally constructive but weak earnings revisions show little evidence of a fundamental inflection.

UK: Case for revisiting underweight UK allocations. The market has returned about 167% since the March 2020 low, trades below long-term average valuations, roughly three-quarters of earnings come from overseas, and mid and small caps are now keeping pace with large caps this year. Takeover activity and buybacks are strong and domestic fund outflows are slowing.

UK Autumn Budget was received constructively. The bank corporation tax surcharge was less onerous than feared and does not detract from the case for large domestic banks. FTSE All Share rose 1.1% in October and the composite PMI hit an eight-month high.

Emerging markets fell sharply. India bucked the trend on low AI exposure and domestic inflows. Brazil fell after Lula's re-election renewed fiscal concerns, Mexico advanced, and Gulf markets fell on geopolitical risk.

Middle East energy shock: disruption to the Strait of Hormuz raised costs for energy importers and benefited commodity exporters, widening the gap between North Asia and energy-dependent South and Southeast Asia. Oil rose, precious and industrial metals weakened on elevated US yields.

Earnings scorecard (FY2028 vs IBES): most bullish on APxJ (+3.9%) and communication services (+7.0% globally), most bearish on EMEA/LATAM (-7.2%) and materials (-11.0% globally). Global net is +2.1% vs IBES.

Quantitative tactical scorecard stays Risk ON. It upgrades the Netherlands and Italy and downgrades the US (to strong underweight), Germany (to neutral), Sweden, Japan (to neutral) and Australia (to strong underweight).

US sector quant signals: staples to overweight, materials to overweight, energy reverses last month's upgrade, real estate strong underweight. Europe: industrials to strong overweight, energy to overweight, communication services and discretionary downgraded, real estate strong underweight.

Fidelity favours companies combining structural demand with strong balance sheets, visible cash generation and demonstrable returns on investment. The AI buildout may shift from a sharp boom to a longer, more differentiated expansion.

sector_views.rationale: Demand strong but near-term estimates and leveraged infrastructure providers face pressure if power and data-centre deployment lags chip output.
Leadership broadened toward these areas in October. US quant model moves staples and materials to overweight.
Led October gains on Middle East tensions, but US quant model reversed its energy upgrade on weaker flows. European quant model moves energy to overweight.
Quant model has Europe industrials at strong overweight on better flows, quality and growth signals. Power infrastructure, defence and data-centre exposure proved resilient.
Quant models have US and Europe real estate at strong underweight on weak flows.
Below-average valuations, broadening leadership, strong shareholder returns and takeover activity strengthen the case for revisiting underweights.

earnings_insights: S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth around 30% (reported season), most companies beat estimates.
STOXX 600 Q3 earnings growth around 28%, concentrated in energy and technology, with only 42% of companies beating expectations.

Fidelity FY2028 earnings growth estimate vs IBES: US +3.0%, Europe -0.1%, APxJ +3.9%, Japan -1.6%, EMEA/LATAM -7.2%, China +0.3%, Global +2.1%. Absolute: US 16.1%, Europe 8.7%, APxJ 12.2%, Japan 10.9%, EMEA/LATAM 1.9%, China 14.1%, Global 13.1%.
FY2028 sector vs IBES (Global): communication services +7.0%, IT +6.9%, industrials +3.5%, materials -11.0%, energy -5.2%, staples -2.2%.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix commentary points to robust high-bandwidth memory demand and tight capacity.
UK: roughly three-quarters of UK earnings are generated overseas.

macro_indicators.interpretation: BoJ held after September's hike with a tightening bias. Supports financials, raises the hurdle for highly valued growth stocks.
Outperformed US markets on defensive and value rotation.
UK rose on resilient activity and earnings.
Manufacturing and services both strengthened, but input cost inflation accelerated, keeping rate uncertainty in focus.
Further tightening possible if price pressures persist.
De-rating of growth and AI stocks on higher global yields and risk-off.

macro_indicators.indicator: MSCI Asia Pacific ex Japan October return
macro_indicators.interpretation: The report cites two different figures for APxJ. Korea and Taiwan were hardest hit.

risk_factors: Chip production running ahead of data-centre power and permitting could pressure near-term semiconductor estimates and leveraged infrastructure providers.
Higher cost of capital, rising capital intensity, weaker free cash flow and greater debt reliance in AI investment.
Persistent inflation, elevated oil prices and the risk of further policy tightening could pressure US valuations, especially if AI investment does not translate into profit growth.
Fed restrictive bias keeps equities sensitive to rate volatility.
BoJ tightening and yen weakness could add currency and rates risk in Japan.
Middle East disruption and Strait of Hormuz energy shock.
France fiscal and political uncertainty. Brazil fiscal concerns after Lula's re-election.
Smaller earnings surprises mean beats may not be rewarded where valuations discount exceptional growth.
vol_and_positioning: Crowded AI and mega-cap positions corrected in October as breadth improved. Momentum fell 10.2% in USD terms for the month while value rose.
South Korea and Taiwan saw crowded AI positions unwind and foreign selling intensify.
Quant model signal is Risk ON overall despite the US downgrade to strong underweight on flows and technical signals.
UK domestic equity fund net outflows are slowing while international investors show interest. Takeover activity and buybacks are strong.
Japan quant downgrade to neutral reflects short-term momentum and active flows headwinds. Australia drops to strong underweight on total flows and momentum.
geopolitical: Middle East tensions lifted oil prices in October and revived inflation and policy concerns in Europe and Japan.
Disruption to the Strait of Hormuz raised costs for energy importers and benefited commodity exporters, widening the gap between North Asia and South and Southeast Asia.
Political and local resistance to data-centre development adds constraints around power, permitting and construction.
US midterm election results intensified the AI-infrastructure debate.
France: political and fiscal uncertainty weighed on financials as sovereign spreads widened vs Germany.
Brazil: President Lula's re-election renewed fiscal concerns and equities erased earlier gains.
UK: political uncertainty after the recent leadership change eased following an uneventful Autumn Budget.
Gulf markets fell as geopolitical risks overshadowed solid earnings.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong underlying demand, capacity-constrained advanced processors and memory, strong cloud growth, expanding hyperscaler backlogs, and robust HBM demand per Samsung and SK Hynix.
tension_points.bear_case: Chip output may temporarily outrun data-centre power and permitting, pressuring near-term semiconductor estimates and leveraged infrastructure providers, while capex raises free cash flow and financing concerns.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that data centres cannot secure power and come online at the pace of chip production, or earnings failing to translate AI investment into sustainable profit growth.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI demand remains strong, but the risk is chip production running ahead of data-centre power availability, which could flatten and extend the cycle.
theme_stances.evidence: chip production could temporarily run ahead of the pace at which data centres

theme_stances.key_argument: Attractive valuations, improving sentiment and strong shareholder returns strengthen the case for revisiting underweight UK allocations.
theme_stances.evidence: the greater risk may increasingly be remaining underweight UK equities
